title: Does order matter?
objectives: Choose between ordered and unordered counts and convert between them.
Use $\binom{n}{k}$, its symmetry and Pascal's rule.

screens.prose: You can hold two of four stocks, A, B, C and D, in equal amounts. Holding A and B is the same position as holding B and A.
screens.question: How many different pairs of stocks could you hold?

hints.text: List the pairs that include A.
A can go with B, C or D.
A gives 3 pairs. B gives 2 new ones, with C or D. Then C with D.

feedback.correct: Six pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the pairs, and count A with B only once.

byKey.ordered: You counted A then B and B then A as different. They are the same holding.
byKey.square: You paired a stock with itself. A pair needs two different stocks.
byKey.four: You counted the stocks. Each pair is two of them together.
byKey.added: You added 4 and 4. Count the pairs themselves: AB, AC and so on.

explain.text: A pairs with 3 others, B with 2 new ones, and C with 1 more: $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$. The pair AB is the same as BA. Next we see how this links to picking in order.

canvas.caption: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD

screens.prose: Now pick one stock first and then a second. Each cell is an ordered pick: row B, column A means B first, then A. A stock cannot be picked twice, so the diagonal is greyed out.
screens.question: Tap every cell that ends with you holding A and B.

hints.text: A and B can be picked in two orders.
Look in row A and in row B.

feedback.correct: AB and BA both leave you holding A and B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find A then B, and B then A.

byKey.r2c1: You found B then A. A then B, in row A, gives the same holding.
byKey.r1c2: You found A then B. B then A, in row B, gives the same holding.

explain.text: The 12 cells off the diagonal are the ordered picks, $4 \times 3$. Every pair fills two of them, one per order, mirrored across the diagonal. So there are $12 \div 2 = 6$ pairs.

canvas.caption: Each pair once above the diagonal, and again below it

screens.prose: A choice where order does not matter is a **combination**. We write $\binom{4}{2}$, read 4 choose 2. You found $\binom{4}{2} = 12 \div 2 = 6$. Now hold three of the four stocks. In order there are $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ picks.

rows: ABC  ACB  BAC  BCA  CAB  CBA
ABD  ADB  BAD  BDA  DAB  DBA

screens.question: What is $\binom{4}{3}$, the number of different holdings of 3 stocks?

hints.text: How many ordered picks does one holding have?
The holding A, B, C has 6 ordered picks.
Each holding appears 6 times among the 24 picks. Divide 24 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how often one holding appears among the 24 ordered picks, then divide.

byKey.ordered: You counted the ordered picks. Each holding appears 6 times among them.
byKey.halved: You divided by 2, as for pairs. Three stocks can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways.
byKey.thirds: You divided by 3. Three stocks have $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ orders.
byKey.rows-shown: Those are the rows drawn so far. The table stops early: work out how many rows it needs.

explain.text: Each holding of 3 can be picked in $3! = 6$ orders. So the 24 ordered picks hold each holding 6 times: $\binom{4}{3} = 24 \div 6 = 4$. Check: leaving out one stock of four gives 4 holdings.

screens.prose: Each time, you divided the ordered picks by the orders of one group. The table collects your counts. Now there are five stocks, and you hold three.

state.caption: Groups = ordered picks ÷ orders of one group

screens.question: What is $\binom{5}{3}$?

hints.text: How many ordered picks of 3 from 5 are there?
The last row already gives 60 ordered picks.
Each holding of 3 has 6 orders. Divide 60 by 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the ordered picks by the orders of one group of 3.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks. A holding ignores order, so divide by its 6 orders.
byKey.halved: You divided by 2. A group of 3 has $3! = 6$ orders.
byKey.thirds: You divided by 3. A group of 3 has $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ orders.

explain.text: There are $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ ordered picks, and each holding appears $3! = 6$ times. So $\binom{5}{3} = 60 \div 6 = 10$. The divisor is always the orders of the chosen group.

screens.prose: Here are the counts $\binom{5}{0}$ to $\binom{5}{5}$, and below them $\binom{6}{0}$ to $\binom{6}{6}$. Each entry in the lower row is the sum of the two above it. This is part of **Pascal's triangle**.
screens.question: What is $\binom{6}{2}$, the missing entry?

hints.text: Which two entries sit just above the gap?
The gap sits under 5 and 10.
Add them: $\binom{6}{2} = \binom{5}{1} + \binom{5}{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two entries just above the gap.

byKey.middle: That is $\binom{6}{3}$, the middle entry. The gap is one place to its left.
byKey.copied: You copied the entry above. Each lower entry adds the two above it.
byKey.ordered: That is $6 \times 5$, the ordered picks. Halve it, or add the two entries above.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied 5 by 10. The rule adds the two entries above.

explain.text: Pairs from 6 stocks either include stock F or not. With F, pick 1 more from 5: $\binom{5}{1} = 5$. Without F, pick 2 from 5: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$; so $\binom{6}{2} = 15$.

screens.prose: Each row reads the same from both ends: $\binom{6}{2} = \binom{6}{4} = 15$. Choosing 2 stocks to hold is the same as choosing 4 to leave out. Now look at the ends of the rows.
screens.question: How many ways can you choose all 6 stocks? And how many ways to choose none?

options.why: You counted one way per stock. Taking all 6 is one holding; taking none is one empty holding.
720 is $6!$, the orders of all six. A holding ignores order, so all six is one holding.
Choosing nothing is still a choice: the empty holding. There is exactly one.

hints.text: Look at the first and last entries of each row.
Every row starts and ends with 1.
Taking everything leaves no choice. Taking nothing also leaves no choice: one way each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the ends of the lower row.

byKey.six-zero: You counted one way per stock. Taking all 6 is one holding; taking none is one empty holding.
byKey.none-impossible: Choosing nothing is still a choice: the empty holding. There is exactly one.

explain.text: Holding all six stocks is a single holding, and holding none is the single empty holding. The formula agrees: $\binom{6}{6} = \tfrac{6!}{6!\,0!} = 1$, using $0! = 1$. Symmetry links the two ends: choosing all to hold is choosing none to leave out.

screens.prose: From 8 analysts, a fund makes two choices. A risk committee of 3 has equal votes. A podium awards gold, silver and bronze. Kim writes 336 for both.
screens.question: Which pair of counts is right?

options.why: That is Kim's answer. The podium is ordered, so 336 fits it. A committee ignores order, so its 336 ordered picks count each committee 6 times.
You swapped the two methods. The committee ignores order and the podium does not.
The committee is right. But swapping gold and silver changes the podium, so order counts there.

hints.text: Does swapping two people change the committee? Does it change the podium?
Gold to Ana and silver to Ben differs from the swap. A committee of Ana and Ben does not.
Ordered picks: $8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$. The committee divides by $3! = 6$.

feedback.correct: Order matters on the podium, not on the committee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each choice, whether swapping two people makes a different outcome.

byKey.kim: You used ordered picks for both, as Kim did. A committee ignores order, so 336 counts each committee 6 times.
byKey.swapped: You used ordered picks for the committee and unordered ones for the podium. It is the other way round.

explain.text: Swapping two medallists changes the podium, so it keeps all $8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$ orders. Swapping two committee members changes nothing, so divide by $3! = 6$: $\binom{8}{3} = 56$. Kim used ordered picks for both, so her committee count is 6 times too big.

screens.prose: Each time, you divided the ordered picks by the $k!$ orders of the chosen group. $$\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$$ Swapping $k$ and $n-k$ leaves it unchanged, so $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$. Choosing who is in chooses who is out.
screens.question: Which equals $\binom{9}{7}$?

options.why: That counts ordered picks of 2. Divide by the $2!$ orders as well.
You swapped top and bottom. You cannot choose 9 items from 7.
You took 2 from 7. Leaving 2 out of 9 is the same as keeping 7 of 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choosing 7 to keep is the same as choosing the 2 to leave out.

explain.text: Every choice of 7 to keep leaves exactly 2 out, and the other way round. So $\binom{9}{7} = \binom{9}{2} = \tfrac{9 \times 8}{2} = 36$. The formula shows it too: $\tfrac{9!}{7!\,2!}$ either way.

screens.prose: We derive $\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$ the way you counted: ordered picks, then divide. Each line carries its reason.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Ordered picks of $k$ from $n$: $\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$, by the multiplication rule
Each group of $k$ appears $k!$ times among them, once per order of its members
So $\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!} = \binom{n}{k} \times k!$, counting the same picks group by group

hints.text: Start from something you can count directly.
The ordered picks come first; the groups come from them.
Count ordered picks, say how often each group appears, write the equation, then divide.

feedback.correct: Count in order, then divide out the orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the ordered picks and end by dividing.

byKey.divide: Dividing by $k!$ is the last step. It needs the equation first.
byKey.equation: The equation uses the fact that each group appears $k!$ times. State that first.

explain.text: You counted ordered picks, noticed each group appears $k!$ times, and divided. With $n = 5$ and $k = 3$: $\tfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$ picks, and $60 \div 3! = 10$, your count. The formula is symmetric in $k$ and $n-k$, which is the symmetry of each row.

screens.prose: A risk team checks the correlation of every pair of assets in a 20-asset portfolio. The grid shows the idea for 6 of them: a pair needs one cell, and the diagonal pairs an asset with itself.
screens.question: How many pairs must the team check for all 20 assets?

hints.text: Is the pair (asset 3, asset 7) different from (asset 7, asset 3)?
Correlation is symmetric, so order does not matter.
Count ordered picks, $20 \times 19$, then halve.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count pairs of two different assets, each pair once.

byKey.ordered: You counted both orders. The correlation of 3 with 7 is that of 7 with 3, so halve.
byKey.whole: You counted the whole $20 \times 20$ grid, diagonal and both halves. Keep one half.
byKey.diagonal: You kept the diagonal. An asset's correlation with itself is always 1, so skip it.
byKey.assets: That is the number of assets. Each one pairs with 19 others.

explain.text: Each pair is one cell above the diagonal. There are $20 \times 19 = 380$ ordered picks, and each pair appears twice: $\binom{20}{2} = 190$. With 6 assets the same count gives the 15 shaded cells.

screens.prose: A screen picks 3 stocks at random from a shortlist of 10 to build a basket. Every basket of 3 is equally likely. Two of the 10, RIO and AAL, are miners.
screens.question: What is the chance the basket holds both miners? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{15}$, such as $\tfrac{8}{120}$.

hints.text: How many baskets are there in all? How many hold both miners?
There are $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ baskets.
A basket with both miners needs 1 more stock from the other 8. So 8 baskets of 120.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count all baskets, then the baskets that contain both miners.

byKey.ordered: You counted the good baskets unordered but all baskets in order. Use the same kind of count for both.
byKey.one-miner: That is the chance of one particular pick being a miner. Both must end up in the basket.
byKey.square: You multiplied $\tfrac{1}{10}$ by itself, as if the picks were put back. Count baskets instead.

explain.text: All baskets: $\binom{10}{3} = 120$. Baskets with both miners: choose the third stock from the other 8, so 8. The chance is $\tfrac{8}{120} = \tfrac{1}{15}$, about 6.7%.

canvas.caption: One of the 8 baskets with both miners

ideas: Ordered picks count each group once per order of its members, so divide by $k!$ to count groups.
$\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$: choosing who is in is choosing who is out, and $\binom{n}{0} = \binom{n}{n} = 1$.
Pascal's rule: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k}$, split by whether one item is chosen.

formula.name: Combinations
formula.note: Ordered picks $\tfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$ divided by the $k!$ orders of each group.

summary.trap: Ask whether swapping two chosen items gives a different outcome. A committee: no, use $\binom{n}{k}$. A podium: yes, keep the order.

quiz.prose: A fund builds an equal-weighted basket of 3 stocks from a shortlist of 10.
quiz.question: How many different baskets are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered picks, then divide by the orders of one basket.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks. The weights are equal, so the order of picking does not matter: divide by 6.
byKey.repeats: You allowed a stock twice and kept order, $10^3$. Neither applies to a basket.
byKey.thirty: You multiplied 10 by 3. Count the picks stage by stage, then divide by $3!$.

explain.text: Ordered picks: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$. Each basket appears $3! = 6$ times among them. So there are $720 \div 6 = 120$ baskets.

quiz.prose: A league table of 10 strategies awards 1st, 2nd and 3rd place by return.
quiz.question: How many different top-three results are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does swapping 1st and 2nd give a different result?

byKey.unordered: You used a combination. Swapping 1st and 2nd changes the result, so keep all the orders.
byKey.repeats: A strategy cannot take two places. Each place has one fewer to choose from.

explain.text: First place has 10 choices, second 9, third 8. The places are different, so we keep every order: $720$. A combination would count only which three made the top, 120.

quiz.prose: A desk keeps 13 of its 15 signals and drops the rest.
quiz.question: How many ways can it choose the 13 to keep?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choosing 13 to keep is choosing 2 to drop.

byKey.ordered-two: You counted the 2 dropped signals in order, $15 \times 14$. Dropping A and B is the same as dropping B and A.
byKey.fifteen: That counts dropping one signal. Two are dropped.

explain.text: Each choice of 13 to keep fixes the 2 to drop. So $\binom{15}{13} = \binom{15}{2} = \tfrac{15 \times 14}{2} = 105$. Symmetry turned a big count into a small one.

quiz.prose: You pick 2 of 6 stocks at random. Every pair is equally likely.
quiz.question: What is the chance that one particular stock, BP, is in your pair? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{3}$, such as $\tfrac{5}{15}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count all pairs, then the pairs that contain BP.

byKey.one-pick: That is the chance for one pick. You make two picks, so BP has two chances to be chosen.

explain.text: There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ pairs. BP pairs with each of the other 5 stocks, so 5 pairs contain it. The chance is $\tfrac{5}{15} = \tfrac{1}{3}$.
